growth_story.headline: Finland grew fast on electronics until 2008, then stalled as Nokia and paper faded and new shocks hit; income per person is back near its 2006 level.
growth_story.arc: Finland began the 1990s in a deep slump: income per person fell 6.4 percent in 1991 as trade with the Soviet Union collapsed and a banking crisis followed, so growth averaged only 0.7 percent a year over 1990–1997. Recovery came through exports and a fast-growing electronics industry led by Nokia, and from 1998 to 2007 income per person grew 3.5 percent a year. Income per person peaked in 2008, fell 8.5 percent in 2009, and then fell again from 2012 to 2014 as Nokia and the paper industry declined. Since 2008 growth has averaged -0.1 percent a year, and in 2025 income per person was 3.1 percent below its 2008 peak, about where it first was in 2006. In recent years the IMF points to lost trade with Russia after the invasion of Ukraine, higher interest rates that hit housing and construction, a downturn in 2023, and stagnant labor productivity. Over 2016–2025 growth averaged 0.6 percent a year, below the 1.3 median of similar economies.

threads.title: Soviet collapse and banking crisis
threads.text: A lending boom in the late 1980s ended in 1990, and the loss of Soviet trade deepened the fall. Bankruptcies led to a banking crisis, and income per person shrank in 1991, 1992 and 1993 before growth returned in 1994.

since_last_year.text: Over the past year the IMF reported that the recovery from the 2023 downturn stayed slow, that unemployment kept rising as more people looked for work, and that public debt kept climbing. In the data, income per person fell 0.3 percent in 2025, its third straight year of decline.

growth_story.tension: The IMF describes a slow recovery since the 2023 downturn, but income per person fell in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025. Part of the gap may be people: the IMF reports immigration adding to the labor force, so a little more output is shared among more residents.
